A kind of paper note from Sichuan in Song China, and the first paper money issued by a government. In 1024 the Song state took over notes that merchants in Chengdu had already been printing.

Sichuan used heavy iron coins, which were clumsy for big trades. In the early 11th century, merchant houses began taking deposits of coin and handing out paper receipts that people traded as money. When some houses failed to pay out, the government stepped in. It set up an official note bureau, limited how many notes could circulate and charged a fee to swap coin for paper. Notes were issued for set terms and stamped with several seals to stop forgery.

What followed:

  • Paper money spread across the Song state under other names.
  • The government soon printed more than it could back, and the notes lost value: an early lesson in inflation.
  • The Yuan made paper the main money of their empire, which amazed Marco Polo.
  • The early Ming tried paper too, but it collapsed, and China turned to silver.

Europe did not have government paper money until the 17th century. John Law's scheme in France in 1716 to 1720 repeated many of the Song's lessons.
